newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-AUSTRALIA TRANSPORT - Europeans jockey for fast train deal.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-AUSTRALIA TRANSPORT - Europeans jockey for fast train deal.

text.p: Rival consortiums planning a very fast train (VFT) between Sydney and Canberra will be out to convince investors of their commercial viability following a government decision to call for tenders.
The project has attracted interest from France's high-speed TGV train, Germany's new magnetic levitation train, and older tilt-train technology that could operate on existing track.
Prime Minister John Howard last week stressed that any government involvement would be on the basis of no net cost to the taxpayer, echoing earlier comments by New South Wales premier Bob Carr.

"What will make this operate will be a financial model that shows a profit for someone with a reasonable fare and a good time," says Nick Cameron, general manager sales and marketing at ABB-Daimler Benz Australia Pty Ltd (ADtranz).
A high-speed link would cut the time for a one-way journey to Canberra to one to two hours, depending on the technology chosen.
The benefits, say tourism lobby group the Tourism Task Force, include bringing Canberra to within a day trip from Sydney, and relieving pressure on Sydney airport.
Speedrail, a joint venture between privately-owned Speedrail Pty Ltd and Franco-British group GEC-Alsthom, is promoting the TGV, which has been operating in France for 15 years.

It proposes a non-stop 80-minute journey, with a train every hour at A$75 for a one-way trip, about half the standard airfare. Trains would run at 300 km/h between the outskirts of Sydney and Canberra.
The hi-tech opposition comes from Europe's Transrapid consortium. Transrapid is made up of ADtranz, Siemens AG and Thyssen Industrie AG.
ADtranz itself is a joint venture between Asea Brown Boveri and Daimler-Benz Transportation.
Transrapid proposes a 58-minute three-stop journey using magnetic levitation propulsion technology, which would allow the train to hover above a slim rail at a cruising speed of 400-450 km/h.

Transrapid has won its first contract for the 290 km Hamburg-Berlin route, due to start running in 2005, and Bonn hopes the train will become a standard-bearer for the world's next generation of high-speed trains.
Transrapid consortium member ADtranz has also expressed interest in a tilt-train project, which would be cheaper but slower than the other two options.
Its proposal would aim for a travel time of 90 minutes, with a total construction cost about a third of Speedrail's.
Other tilt-train proposals could come from Spain and Italy.
For all participants, the combination of travel time, cost and passenger numbers will determine commercial feasibility.
Critics have questioned whether a purpose-built rail link to can provide investors with an adequate return without some form of government subsidy.
A Canberra-Sydney project would link a large city and a medium-sized city, noted one transport analyst, compared with the larger population centres linked in Europe.
ADtranz's Cameron said he was also concerned of the consequences of financial failure. "That could kill high-speed rail travel for good," he said.
The two hi-tech proposals, however, believe passenger numbers should offer suitable returns.
"The view we are getting from the investment community is that it will be the time that is important, says Transrapid representative Gerrard Brennan of Canberra consultants Forbes Mason Brennan.
"And they are looking at a time of about an hour to make it competitive with air," he said,
Transrapid has released no costings, but Brennan said the group would seek funding both in Australia and overseas.
Speedrail has costed its project at A$2.4 billion, with GEC Alsthom agreeing to contribute up to A$200 million of a planned A$500 million equity component.
Speedrail managing director Dale Budd said the group was in talks with a number of large Australian companies interested in joining the consortium.
The new make-up of the consortium was expected to be finalised by the time Speedrail responded to the call for expressions of interest, expected in January.
Budd said Speedrail believed it could attract four million one-way trips a year, about a third of which would be to Goulburn and the Southern Highlands on a separate service.
"We are very confident that the numbers do work and that we can finance it in the private sector," he said.
